title: Scaling the data layer
description: Replicate, partition, and keep data correct once one database isn't enough.

lessons.title: Replication
lessons.summary: Copies of your data for read scale and survival: leaders, followers, lag, failover, and quorums.

steps.prompt: Your Postgres primary is at 90% CPU, and 95% of its queries are reads. What's the cheapest effective first move?
options: Add read replicas and send reads to them
Shard the data across four databases
Add a second leader that also accepts writes
Migrate to a NoSQL database
steps.answer: Add read replicas and send reads to them
steps.why: Each replica holds a full copy of the data and can serve reads, so read capacity grows with every replica you add while writes still go to one place.

misconceptions.Shard the data across four databases: Sharding also works, but it's a big, hard-to-undo change. When the load is reads, replicas solve it for far less effort.
misconceptions.Add a second leader that also accepts wr: A second write leader brings write conflicts and solves nothing here: the pressure comes from reads, not writes.
misconceptions.Migrate to a NoSQL database: A migration costs months, and NoSQL stores still need replicas or partitions to scale reads.

steps.title: Leader and followers
steps.body:
One node, the **leader**, accepts every write and streams its change log to **followers** (read replicas), which apply the changes in the same order. Reads can go to any copy.

**Synchronous** replication waits for a follower to confirm before acknowledging a write. **Asynchronous** acknowledges at once and copies later: faster, but the newest writes are lost if the leader dies.

steps.context: A payments ledger runs one leader and three followers, each in a different zone.
steps.prompt: An acknowledged payment must survive even if the leader's disk dies a second later. Which setup fits best?
options: Asynchronous replication to all three followers
Synchronous to one follower, asynchronous to the other two
Synchronous to all three followers
No replication, but hourly backups
steps.answer: Synchronous to one follower, asynchronous to the other two
steps.why: Waiting for one follower guarantees every acknowledged write exists on two machines, while the async followers can't stall writes. This is often called **semi-synchronous** replication.

misconceptions.Asynchronous replication to all three fo: Async acknowledges before any copy exists. If the leader dies, its newest writes die with it.
misconceptions.Synchronous to all three followers: Durable, but now any one slow or failed follower blocks every write. Availability gets worse as you add replicas.
misconceptions.No replication, but hourly backups: Hourly backups can lose up to an hour of payments, and restoring takes far longer than failing over.

steps.title: Replication lag
steps.body:
Async followers trail the leader, usually by milliseconds, but by seconds or more under heavy load. A user posts a comment, refreshes, and the read lands on a lagging replica: the comment seems gone.

Guarantee **read-your-writes** by reading a user's own recent changes from the leader, or from a replica that has caught up to their last write.

steps.prompt: Your app sends most reads to async replicas. Which of these reads should go to the leader instead?

items.text: Showing users their profile right after they edit it
items.why: Read-your-writes: a lagging replica would show the old profile.

items.text: Validating a password-reset token issued two seconds ago
items.why: The token was just written; a replica may not have it yet and would reject a valid link.

items.text: Checking stock inside the transaction that decrements it
items.why: A read that decides a write must see the latest data, or two buyers can claim the last item.

items.text: Rendering the public home page feed
items.why: Nobody notices if it's a second behind.
Heavy scans on a replica keep load off the leader, and a few seconds of lag doesn't matter.

items.text: Showing the like count on a viral post
items.why: An approximate count is fine for display.

steps.why: Send a read to the leader only when staleness causes a visible bug: the user's own fresh writes, data just created, or reads that decide a write. Everything else can scale out on replicas.

steps.context: The leader stops answering heartbeats. After a timeout, the cluster promotes the most up-to-date follower and points writes at it. But the old leader was only cut off by a network glitch, and some app servers are still writing to it.
steps.prompt: Two nodes now accept writes: **split brain**. What prevents it?
options: Fence the old leader so its writes are rejected
Make all replication synchronous
Add more followers
Shorten the failover timeout
steps.answer: Fence the old leader so its writes are rejected
steps.why: Failover is only safe once the old leader is shut out. Fencing does that: a leadership lease that expires, an epoch number that makes storage reject stale leaders, or powering the old node off (STONITH).

misconceptions.Make all replication synchronous: Synchronous replication prevents losing acknowledged writes, but two nodes can still each believe they're the leader.
misconceptions.Add more followers: More followers don't change which nodes accept writes.
misconceptions.Shorten the failover timeout: A shorter timeout triggers more false failovers when the leader is merely slow, which makes split brain *more* likely.

steps.title: More than one writer
steps.body:
**Multi-leader**: several nodes accept writes, often one per region, and sync with each other. Writes are fast, but concurrent edits **conflict** and must be merged.

**Leaderless** (Dynamo-style, like Cassandra): each write goes to N replicas and succeeds after W acks; reads ask R replicas. If **W + R > N**, at least one replica you read has the latest write.

rows: Stale reads when W + R ≤ N

steps.prompt: A leaderless store keeps N = 3 replicas of each key. Which settings guarantee that a read overlaps the latest successful write? Select all that apply.
steps.why: Any W nodes and any R nodes out of N must share at least one node when W + R > N; both 2 + 2 and 3 + 1 make 4 > 3. W = 3 is fragile, though: a write fails if any replica is down, which is why W = R = 2 is the common choice.

misconceptions.W = 1, R = 2: 1 + 2 = 3 equals N but doesn't exceed it: the single node that took the write can be exactly the one you skip.
misconceptions.W = 1, R = 1: Fast, but a read can easily land on a replica the write never reached.

steps.prompt: Match each problem to its fix.
pairs: Users can't see a comment they just posted
Read their own recent writes from the leader
Two nodes accept writes after a failover
Users on three continents need fast writes
No acknowledged write may be lost on failover
steps.why: Each replication choice fixes one problem and brings its own: replicas bring lag, failover risks split brain, multi-leader brings conflicts, and synchronous followers slow writes.

steps.context: A recipe site serves 50K reads/sec but only 500 writes/sec. The same popular recipes are read over and over.
steps.prompt: Design the data path: scale reads without losing a single source of truth for writes.

nodes.why: Several app servers need one stable entry point that spreads requests and skips dead servers.
Read replicas take the read load off the leader.

edges.why: Writes go to the leader, the single source of truth.
Reads go to replicas; that's where the read scaling comes from.
Replicas stay current by applying the leader's change log.
Popular recipes repeat, so a cache serves them from memory before any database is touched.

paths.why: Requests enter through the load balancer, never straight to one server.

forbidden.why: Clients never talk to a database directly: no auth, no validation, no connection pooling.

steps.why: Writes funnel to one leader, so there's a single source of truth; reads fan out across a cache and replicas, which is where 99% of this traffic goes. Replica reads can lag, so a user's own fresh edits should still be read from the leader.

lessons.title: Sharding
lessons.summary: Split data across machines: partitioning schemes, consistent hashing, shard keys, and what sharding costs.

steps.context: Your database holds 30 TB and takes 50K writes/sec at peak. One machine can't keep up with either.
steps.prompt: Why won't adding read replicas fix this?
options: Every replica stores all 30 TB and applies every write
Replicas can't serve reads while the leader is busy
Replication lag makes replicas unusable at this size
Replication only works for SQL databases
steps.answer: Every replica stores all 30 TB and applies every write
steps.why: Replication multiplies copies of the whole dataset, so each node still carries 100% of the data and 100% of the writes. To divide the load, you divide the data: shard it.

misconceptions.Replicas can't serve reads while the lea: They can; serving reads is their main job. The problem here is storage and writes, which replicas copy rather than split.
misconceptions.Replication lag makes replicas unusable: Lag is real, but it isn't the blocker. Even a perfectly current replica must store all 30 TB and absorb all 50K writes/sec.
misconceptions.Replication only works for SQL databases: Nearly every database replicates, SQL and NoSQL alike.

steps.title: Splitting the data
steps.body:
**Vertical partitioning** splits by table or column: profiles in one database, orders in another. **Horizontal partitioning**, or **sharding**, splits by row: every shard has the same schema but owns a slice of the keys.

Vertical splits buy some room. Sharding keeps scaling, because each shard stores and writes only its slice.

left.title: Vertical partitioning
points: One huge table still hits a ceiling

right.title: Horizontal (sharding)
points: Each shard owns a range or hash of keys
Writes and storage scale with shard count

steps.prompt: How many shards do you need?
steps.hint: Work out the shards needed for storage and for writes separately.
solution: Take the larger need: 15 shards (many teams round up to 16)
steps.why: Shard count is set by whichever resource runs out first, here storage. Plan for growth too, because adding shards later means moving live data.

steps.title: Range or hash?
steps.body:
**Range partitioning** gives each shard a contiguous key range (A–F, G–M…). Range scans are cheap, but sequential keys like timestamps pile onto the newest shard.

**Hash partitioning** sends each key to shard `hash(key) mod N`. Load spreads evenly, but a range query has to ask every shard.

rows: Cheap: one or a few shards

steps.prompt: With `hash(key) mod N`, you grow from 4 shards to 5. Roughly what share of keys must move to a different shard?
options: About 20%
About 80%
Exactly 25%
None: only new keys use the new shard
steps.hint: A key stays only if its remainder mod 4 equals its remainder mod 5.
steps.why: A key stays put only if `hash mod 4` equals `hash mod 5`, which holds for just 4 of every 20 hash values. Moving 80% of your data to add one shard is why real systems use consistent hashing.

misconceptions.About 20%: That's the ideal: the new shard's fair share. Mod N moves far more, because changing N changes almost every key's remainder.
misconceptions.Exactly 25%: One in four is each shard's share *before* the change, not how many keys move.
misconceptions.None: only new keys use the new shard: Existing keys' remainders change when N changes, so their lookups go to the wrong shard unless the data moves.

steps.title: Consistent hashing
steps.body:
**Consistent hashing** puts shards and keys on a ring of hash values; each key belongs to the next shard clockwise. Adding a shard moves only the keys it takes over, about 1/N of the data.

Each machine gets many **virtual nodes** around the ring, which evens out load and spreads a dead machine's keys across all the others.

steps.context: 1M sensors each send a reading every 10 seconds. The main query: "readings for device X over the last 24 hours."
steps.prompt: Good or bad shard key for the readings table?

items.why: A million distinct values spread writes evenly, and each device's readings sit on one shard for the main query.
Keeps a device's day together, so the 24-hour query touches at most two partitions, and caps how big any partition grows.
Every reading being written now lands in the newest range: one shard takes all the writes.
Three values can feed at most three shards, however many you buy.
Low cardinality, and the busiest region becomes a permanent hot shard.
Writes spread perfectly, but "device X's last 24 hours" now has to ask every shard.

steps.why: A good shard key has many distinct values, spreads load evenly, and keeps your most common query on a single shard.

steps.title: What sharding costs
steps.body:
Even a good key can be skewed: one celebrity's data can melt its shard while others idle. Queries without the shard key must **scatter** to every shard and **gather** the results. Joins and transactions across shards get hard, and **resharding** means moving live data.

So shard late, and pick a key that keeps most queries on one shard.

rows: Cache it, add replicas, or salt the key
Consistent hashing; many small virtual shards

steps.context: A celebrity with 100M followers posts. Their shard hits 100% CPU serving reads while the other shards sit near 10%.
steps.prompt: What's the best fix?
options: Cache the celebrity's posts and serve reads from the cache
Add more shards
Switch from hash to range partitioning
Re-shard by post timestamp
steps.answer: Cache the celebrity's posts and serve reads from the cache
steps.why: A hot key is a single key, so repartitioning can't split it. Absorb its reads with a cache or extra replicas; if writes are the problem, salt the key (`user#0` … `user#9`) to spread them across shards.

misconceptions.Add more shards: The hot key still maps to exactly one shard. More shards just add idle machines.
misconceptions.Switch from hash to range partitioning: The celebrity's key still lives in one place under any partitioning scheme.
misconceptions.Re-shard by post timestamp: That trades one hotspot for another: every new post would land on the newest shard.

steps.context: A chat app stores billions of messages in 1:1 and group conversations. The hottest query: "load the latest 50 messages in this conversation."
steps.prompt: Pick a shard key for the messages table and justify it.

concepts.label: A conversation's messages live on one shard
Many distinct values spread load evenly
Plans for huge or hot conversations

steps.model: Shard by conversation_id, hashed. The hot query reads one conversation, so all of its messages live on the same shard and the query never scatters to every shard. There are millions of conversations, so hashing spreads load evenly. A huge, busy group chat could still become a hot partition, so I'd add a time bucket to the key, as Discord does with (channel_id, bucket), to cap partition size.
steps.why: Shard on what your hottest query filters by, as long as it has many distinct values. Sharding by user_id would scatter a group chat across many shards, and sharding by timestamp would send every new message to one shard.

lessons.title: Consistency and CAP
lessons.summary: What reads are allowed to return, what partitions force you to give up, and how to choose per feature.

steps.context: You change your profile photo and refresh. You still see the old photo. A friend refreshing a second later sees the new one.
steps.prompt: What most likely happened?
options: Your read hit a replica that hadn't applied the write yet
The write was lost and then retried
The database is corrupted
steps.answer: Your read hit a replica that hadn't applied the write yet
steps.why: With asynchronous replicas, a read can be briefly stale. That's **eventual consistency**: replicas converge, but not instantly. Seeing your *own* change disappear breaks a guarantee called **read-your-writes**.

misconceptions.The write was lost and then retried: A lost write wouldn't show up for your friend a second later either.
misconceptions.The database is corrupted: Corruption doesn't fix itself a second later. Brief staleness that clears on its own is the signature of replication lag.

steps.title: Consistency models
steps.body:
A **consistency model** is a promise about what reads may return. **Linearizable** (strong): every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. **Eventual**: replicas converge once writes stop, but reads may be stale meanwhile.

In between sit cheaper guarantees: **causal**, **read-your-writes**, and **monotonic reads**.

rows: Every read sees the latest write
A reply shows up before its question
You always see your own writes
Your new post vanishes on refresh
Time never goes backwards for you

steps.context: Alice comments on a post. Bob refreshes and sees her comment. He refreshes again, a more-lagged replica answers, and the comment is gone.
steps.prompt: What is the *cheapest* guarantee that prevents this?
options: Monotonic reads
Read-your-writes
Linearizability
Eventual consistency
steps.why: Monotonic reads promises a user never sees older data after newer data. A cheap way to get it is to route each user to the same replica, for example by hashing the user ID.

misconceptions.Read-your-writes: Read-your-writes protects *your own* writes. Bob is reading Alice's comment; his problem is seeing time go backwards.
misconceptions.Linearizability: It would prevent this, but it's far stronger than needed and costs latency on every read. Monotonic reads is enough.
misconceptions.Eventual consistency: This *is* eventual consistency: it's the weak guarantee that allowed the anomaly.

steps.title: CAP, stated correctly
steps.body:
Networks **partition**: links fail and nodes can't reach each other. During a partition, a replicated system must choose: refuse some requests to stay **consistent** (linearizable), or answer them all and risk stale or conflicting data to stay **available**.

With no partition, you can have both. "Pick two of three" misleads: partitions aren't optional.

left.title: CP during a partition
points: Nodes cut off from the majority refuse requests
Nobody sees stale or conflicting data

right.title: AP during a partition
points: Reads may be stale; writes may conflict

steps.context: A partition splits a 5-node cluster into groups of 3 and 2. A client connected to the 2-node side sends a write. System A is CP; system B is AP.
steps.prompt: What happens?
options: A rejects the write; B accepts it and reconciles after the partition heals
A accepts the write; B rejects it
Both accept it, and both stay linearizable
Both reject it until the partition heals
steps.answer: A rejects the write; B accepts it and reconciles after the partition heals
steps.why: The 2-node side can't reach a majority. CP refuses rather than risk two divergent histories; AP accepts and must reconcile conflicting writes later, with last-write-wins, merges, or CRDTs.

misconceptions.A accepts the write; B rejects it: Reversed. Consistency means refusing what you can't coordinate; availability means answering anyway.
misconceptions.Both accept it, and both stay linearizab: That's exactly what CAP rules out: the 2-node side can't know what the 3-node side accepted meanwhile.
misconceptions.Both reject it until the partition heals: An AP system's whole point is to keep answering on both sides of a partition.

steps.context: Like counts live in an AP store. During a partition, the US side records 120 new likes on a post and the EU side records 80. Both started from 1,000.
steps.prompt: After the partition heals, how should the replicas merge?
options: Keep a count per replica and sum them: 1,200
Last write wins: 1,120 or 1,080, whichever side wrote last
Average the two sides: 1,100
Keep the higher value: 1,120
steps.answer: Keep a count per replica and sum them: 1,200
steps.why: Increments can be merged without loss: each replica counts its own increments, and the total is their sum. That's the idea behind a counter **CRDT**.

misconceptions.Last write wins: 1,120 or 1,080, whichev: Last-write-wins silently throws away one side's likes. It suits overwrites like a display name, not counters.
misconceptions.Average the two sides: 1,100: Averaging loses 100 likes that really happened.
misconceptions.Keep the higher value: 1,120: The EU side's 80 likes would vanish.

steps.title: PACELC: the everyday trade-off
steps.body:
CAP only covers partitions, which are rare. **PACELC** adds the rest of the time: if **P**artitioned, choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency; **E**lse, choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency.

Even on a healthy network, a strongly consistent write must wait for replicas to agree, often across regions, while an eventually consistent one returns at once.

steps.text: During a network [[partition]], a node that can't reach its peers must either refuse requests, keeping [[consistency]], or answer them, keeping [[availability]]. With no partition, PACELC says the trade-off is consistency versus [[latency]], because waiting for replicas to agree takes time.
steps.why: CAP describes behavior during a partition only. PACELC reminds you that strong consistency costs latency on every request, even when the network is fine.

steps.title: Choose per feature
steps.body:
One product needs several consistency levels. Ask what breaks if a read is a second stale. Money moved twice, or one seat sold to two people? You need **strong** consistency. A like count off by three? **Eventual** is fine.

Most screens sit in between: users must never see their own changes vanish, or time run backwards.

left.title: Needs strong
points: Selling the last unit of stock

steps.prompt: Match each feature to the weakest consistency level that keeps it correct.
pairs: Your profile page right after you edit it
Scrolling a feed without posts disappearing
steps.why: Pay for strong consistency only where a stale read causes real damage. Session guarantees like read-your-writes and monotonic reads fix most user-visible glitches far more cheaply.

lessons.title: Transactions across services
lessons.summary: When one transaction spans several services: two-phase commit, sagas, the outbox, and idempotent consumers.

steps.context: Checkout calls the Payments service to charge the card, then the Inventory service to reserve the item. The charge succeeds. The inventory call times out.
steps.prompt: What state is the order in?
options: Unknown: the item may or may not be reserved, and the card is charged either way
Safe: the database rolls back the charge automatically
Failed cleanly: a timeout means the reservation didn't happen
Safe: the load balancer retries the call for you
steps.answer: Unknown: the item may or may not be reserved, and the card is charged either way
steps.why: Across services there's no shared transaction, and a timeout is ambiguous. You need a protocol that either completes every step or explicitly undoes the ones that ran.

misconceptions.Safe: the database rolls back the charge: Each service has its own database. No transaction spans both, so nothing rolls back the charge for you.
misconceptions.Failed cleanly: a timeout means the rese: A timeout only means no reply arrived. The reservation may have succeeded and the response got lost.
misconceptions.Safe: the load balancer retries the call: Blind retries of a non-idempotent call can reserve twice, and they never undo the charge if the item is truly out of stock.

steps.title: ACID stops at the service boundary
steps.body:
Inside one database, a transaction is **atomic** (all or nothing), **consistent** (rules like "balance ≥ 0" hold), **isolated** (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), and **durable** (committed data survives crashes).

Spread the data over services with separate databases, and no single engine can promise that across them.

left.title: One database
points: The engine rolls back on failure

right.title: Several services
points: Each service commits on its own
Nothing undoes a step that already committed
The network can fail between any two steps

steps.prompt: Which ACID property prevents each failure?
pairs: A crash between the debit and the credit leaves money missing
Two concurrent transfers both read the same old balance
A committed order vanishes after a power cut
A transfer leaves an account below its allowed minimum
steps.why: Atomicity handles partial failure, isolation handles concurrency, durability handles crashes after commit, and consistency is the application's invariants, which the other three help protect.

steps.title: Two-phase commit
steps.body:
**2PC** commits across several databases atomically. A **coordinator** asks every participant to **prepare**: write everything durably, hold its locks, and vote. If all vote yes, it logs the decision and tells everyone to **commit**; any no means **abort**.

The catch: a participant that voted yes can't decide alone. If the coordinator dies, it waits, locks held.

steps.prompt: In 2PC, every participant voted yes. Then the coordinator crashed before sending its decision. What can a participant safely do?
options: Wait, holding its locks, until the coordinator recovers
Commit on its own, since it voted yes
Abort on its own after a timeout
Ask the client what to do
steps.answer: Wait, holding its locks, until the coordinator recovers
steps.why: A yes vote is a promise to commit if told to, so a prepared participant is stuck "in doubt" with its locks held. That blocking, plus the cost of holding locks across services, is why 2PC is rare between microservices.

misconceptions.Commit on its own, since it voted yes: It knows only its own vote. Another participant may have voted no, so the decision could be abort.
misconceptions.Abort on its own after a timeout: The coordinator may already have told another participant to commit. Aborting alone breaks atomicity.
misconceptions.Ask the client what to do: The client doesn't know the decision either; only the coordinator's log does.

steps.title: Sagas
steps.body:
A **saga** splits one business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, one per service, each committed on its own. If a step fails, the saga runs **compensating actions** for the steps that already succeeded, in reverse order: refund the payment, release the stock.

No locks span services, but others can see the in-between states.

steps.context: A trip-booking saga books a flight, then a hotel, then a rental car. The car step fails: no cars left.
steps.prompt: Put everything that happens in order.
items: Mark the trip failed and notify the traveler
steps.why: Steps commit one at a time; when one fails, compensations undo the completed steps in reverse. The failed car step committed nothing, so it needs no compensation.

steps.context: Sagas run two ways. **Choreography**: each service reacts to the others' events (`FlightBooked` triggers the hotel service), with no central controller. **Orchestration**: one orchestrator tells each service what to do and tracks the saga's state.
steps.prompt: Your seven-step order saga fails in ways nobody can trace. Which approach helps most?
options: Orchestration: one place defines the sequence and tracks each saga's state
Choreography: fewer components means fewer failures
Two-phase commit across all seven services
Retry every step until it succeeds
steps.answer: Orchestration: one place defines the sequence and tracks each saga's state
steps.why: Choreography suits short sagas with few participants. As a saga grows, an orchestrator, often a workflow engine like Temporal or AWS Step Functions, makes the sequence explicit, observable, and easier to change.

misconceptions.Choreography: fewer components means few: Fewer boxes, but the flow is scattered across event handlers in seven services, which is exactly what makes it hard to trace.
misconceptions.Two-phase commit across all seven servic: Holding locks across seven services for the whole flow multiplies 2PC's blocking problem.
misconceptions.Retry every step until it succeeds: Some failures are permanent, like a declined card. Retrying forever never compensates the steps that already ran.

steps.title: The transactional outbox
steps.body: A service saves an order, then publishes `OrderPlaced` to a broker. Crash between the two and they disagree: a **dual write**. The **outbox** fixes it: insert the event into an `outbox` table in the **same local transaction** as the order. A relay publishes outbox rows; after a crash it may resend, so consumers must be **idempotent**.

steps.text: Writing to the database and then the broker separately is a [[dual write]]: a crash in between loses or invents events. With an outbox, the order and its event commit in [[one local transaction]]. The relay may publish a row twice after a crash, so delivery is [[at-least-once]], and consumers must be [[idempotent]], for example by recording processed [[event IDs]] and skipping repeats.
steps.why: The outbox turns two writes into one local commit, and the relay retries until the broker has the event. Retries mean duplicates, and idempotent consumers make duplicates harmless.

lessons.title: Unique IDs at scale
lessons.summary: Auto-increment, UUIDs, Snowflake IDs, and ticket servers: generating IDs on many machines at once.

steps.prompt: You split your users table across 8 shards, each with its own `AUTO_INCREMENT` counter. What breaks?
options: Different shards hand out the same IDs
Inserts get slower than on one database
IDs run out sooner
Nothing: each shard is independent
steps.answer: Different shards hand out the same IDs
steps.why: Auto-increment is unique only inside one database. You can patch it (MySQL's `auto_increment_increment` and `auto_increment_offset` give shard k the IDs k, k+8, k+16…), but most systems switch to an ID scheme built for many machines.

misconceptions.Nothing: each shard is independent: Each shard counts 1, 2, 3… on its own, so user 42 exists eight times. Every URL, cache key, and foreign key that says "user 42" becomes ambiguous.
misconceptions.Inserts get slower than on one database: Each shard's counter is local and fast. Speed isn't the issue; uniqueness is.
misconceptions.IDs run out sooner: A 64-bit counter won't run out. The problem is that eight counters overlap.

steps.title: What a good ID needs
steps.body:
A single database's **auto-increment** is simple and ordered, but every insert in the system must go through it: a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

At scale you want IDs that are **unique** across machines, generated **locally**, **compact** (64 bits fits a `BIGINT`), and **roughly time-sorted**, so new rows append to the end of the index.

steps.context: A **UUIDv4** is 128 bits, 122 of them random. Any server can generate one with no coordination.
steps.prompt: A team switches a large MySQL (InnoDB) table's primary key from auto-increment to UUIDv4. Inserts get much slower. Why?
options: Random keys insert all over the B-tree index, causing page splits and cache misses
Generating each UUID needs a network call
UUIDs collide often at this scale
128-bit values can't be indexed
steps.answer: Random keys insert all over the B-tree index, causing page splits and cache misses
steps.why: InnoDB stores rows in primary-key order. Sequential keys append to the last page, which stays in memory; random keys hit pages all over the index, so pages split and the working set outgrows RAM. Time-ordered IDs, like Snowflake or UUIDv7 (which starts with a millisecond timestamp), avoid this.

misconceptions.Generating each UUID needs a network cal: UUIDv4 is generated locally from random bits; avoiding coordination is its whole appeal.
misconceptions.UUIDs collide often at this scale: You'd need about a billion UUIDs a second for roughly 85 years to reach even a 50% chance of one collision.
misconceptions.128-bit values can't be indexed: They index fine. The problem is *where* each new key lands in the index.

steps.title: Snowflake IDs
steps.body: Twitter's **Snowflake** packs a 64-bit integer: a **41-bit timestamp** in milliseconds since a custom epoch (about 69 years of range), a **10-bit machine ID** (1,024 generators), and a **12-bit sequence** counting IDs within one millisecond, plus an unused sign bit. Each machine generates IDs locally, and sorting by ID roughly sorts by creation time.

left.title: UUIDv4
points: Can be made anywhere, even offline

right.title: Snowflake
points: Each generator needs a unique machine ID
Roughly time-ordered: appends to the index

steps.prompt: What's the most IDs one Snowflake generator can issue per second?
steps.hint: How many values fit in 12 bits?
solution: 4,096 × 1,000 ms = 4,096,000 ≈ 4M IDs per second, per machine
steps.why: The sequence caps how many IDs fit in one millisecond; if it runs out, the generator waits for the next millisecond. Roughly 4M per second per machine is far more than most services need.

steps.title: Ticket servers and ranges
steps.body:
A **ticket server** is a database whose only job is issuing auto-increment numbers. Flickr ran two, one issuing odd IDs and one even, so losing either wasn't fatal.

To skip a round trip per ID, app servers can lease a **range**, say 1,000 IDs at a time, and hand them out from memory. IDs stay unique but only roughly ordered.

steps: Range used up: lease the next

steps.context: NTP corrects a Snowflake generator's clock, moving it back 5 ms.
steps.prompt: What should the generator do?
options: Refuse to issue IDs until its clock passes the last timestamp it used
Keep going: the sequence number keeps IDs unique
Reset the sequence to zero and continue
Pick a new random machine ID
steps.answer: Refuse to issue IDs until its clock passes the last timestamp it used
steps.why: Snowflake remembers the last timestamp it used and won't generate while the clock is behind it. Skew *between* machines doesn't break uniqueness; it only makes cross-machine order approximate, which is why IDs are roughly, not exactly, time-sorted.

misconceptions.Keep going: the sequence number keeps ID: The sequence restarts every millisecond, so replaying those same 5 ms can produce IDs it already issued.
misconceptions.Reset the sequence to zero and continue: Same timestamp, same machine, sequence 0 again: that's exactly how duplicates happen.
misconceptions.Pick a new random machine ID: It could collide with another live generator's ID. Machine IDs are assigned, not guessed.

steps.prompt: Match each ID scheme to its trade-off.
pairs: Simple and ordered, but a bottleneck and single point of failure
No coordination, but 128 bits and random index inserts
128 bits, but time-ordered so inserts append
64-bit and roughly time-sorted, but needs unique machine IDs
A central counter, contacted once per batch
steps.why: Every scheme trades coordination, size, and ordering. Index locality pushes you toward time-ordered IDs; creating IDs with no server at hand pushes you toward UUIDs.

steps.context: A notes app lets people create notes on their phones while offline, syncing to the server later.
steps.prompt: Which ID scheme fits?
options: UUIDs generated on the device
Snowflake, with each phone as a machine
Auto-increment from the server's database
Leased ranges from a ticket server
steps.why: Offline creation rules out anything that needs a server round trip or an assigned machine ID. With 122 random bits, UUIDs need no coordination at all, and UUIDv7 keeps them roughly time-ordered too.

misconceptions.Snowflake, with each phone as a machine: 10 bits allow only 1,024 machine IDs. Millions of phones can't each get a unique one.
misconceptions.Auto-increment from the server's databas: The phone is offline; it can't ask the server for an ID until it syncs.
misconceptions.Leased ranges from a ticket server: It can work if every device leases a range while online, but a brand-new device has none, and you're managing millions of leases.
